McDonald’s said in a statement that its technology does "not automate, coordinate or fix pricing in any way,” but allows franchisees to “make the best decisions for their businesses and customers.” Jeffrey Shinder, an antitrust lawyer who is not involved in the McDonald's case, said cases over algorithmic pricing are testing the law's ability to keep pace with technological change, and could multiply amid a public backlash against AI. "I would expect to see more of them," he said. (This story has been refiled to fix the hyperlink in paragraph 5.)

item.title: US Army report cites systematic failures in 2025 helicopter and jet collision that killed 67
item.description: The collision of an American Airlines regional jet and an Army Black Hawk helicopter near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport last year that killed 67 people was the result of several systemic failures, according to a US Army investigative report seen by Reuters.
item.dc:creator: David Shepardson
item.content:encoded: The collision of an American Airlines regional jet and an Army Black Hawk helicopter near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport last year that killed 67 people was the result of several systemic failures, according to a US Army investigative report seen by Reuters. The previously undisclosed report completed in May made a series of safety recommendations and said the key factor was two broken radio transmissions resulting in the helicopter crew not receiving critical details from air traffic control. The report also found a number of other issues including technical issues with the Black Hawk and a pattern of helicopter crews failing to fly semiannual minimum hours. It said many helicopters in the Army battalion — including the one in the January 2025 collision — did not have Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance systems. The report also said Army work with the Federal Aviation Administration on helicopter incidents in the Washington area before the collision was lacking and a working group "did not discuss airspace violations, near-miss reports, or pilot deviations." National Transportation Safety Board Chair Jennifer Homendy said in an October 1 letter to the Army that it had made significant progress in addressing its recommendations from the collision. It added, however, that it needed to do more work as "the Army's aviation safety system failed to consistently detect, interpret, and act on signals of latent hazards, resulting in degraded safety assurance, organizational learning, and safety culture." The NTSB report on the crash in January found a series of failures by the FAA were largely responsible for the deadliest US aviation disaster in more than two decades. The Army report noted that the helicopter was not providing key safety location data, known as ADS-B Out, due to improper maintenance. After the incident, the Army issued an urgent safety message to inspect all Army aircraft transponders to ensure ADS-B Out functionality, and all 3,600 Army helicopters were inspected by July 2025. The report also noted the Army had not addressed issues that led to the helicopter providing inaccurate altitude data and proposed a series of recommendations to address the issue. It also said the Army needs more advanced night vision equipment for pilots. The Army report also faulted FAA air traffic control for using "non-standard terminology for directing air traffic and providing incomplete traffic advisories." The FAA did not immediately comment. The Army said in a statement on Thursday that it has implemented stronger training and surveillance checks and completed new helicopter safety inspections, and testing on altitude awareness. It also said it was pursuing an FAA data-sharing agreement to help identify potential midair collision risks. The report also called for improved training for military pilots around Washington and Baltimore commercial airports and for reviews of Army helicopter operations near major cities in the United States, South Korea, Japan and Germany. Congress is still debating aviation safety legislation after lawmakers passed competing versions. The family of First Officer Sam Lilley, who was killed in the collision, said the Army report shows "the system failed everyone that night. The Army’s report acknowledges failures involving known altimeter issues, near-miss reporting, training, risk mitigation and safety culture."

item.title: US freezes Microsoft, Adobe, Infosys green-card applications over alleged fraud
item.description: The Trump administration froze on Thursday some green-card filings by Microsoft , Adobe and major IT outsourcers and opened probes into nine top universities, widening a visa crackdown it says targets fraud and protects American jobs.
item.dc:creator: Akash Sriram, Steve Holland
item.content:encoded: The Trump administration froze on Thursday some green-card filings by Microsoft (MSFT.O) , Adobe (ADBE.O) and major IT outsourcers and opened probes into nine top universities, widening a visa crackdown it says targets fraud and protects American jobs. The twin actions mark the broadest strike yet against skilled-worker immigration programs — potentially cutting off a common path to permanent residency for foreign tech workers — while putting some of the country's top research universities on notice. "There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the system more than Microsoft," Vice President JD Vance said. He said the company laid off 6,000 American workers last year while benefiting from 6,300 H-1B temporary worker visas and nearly 3,000 green cards. The announcement about the permanent labor certification process — PERM — came hours before Trump was due to give Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella the National Medal of Technology and Innovation. Under PERM, required for most employment-based green cards, employers must show that hiring a foreign worker will not harm US workers' wages or job opportunities. Microsoft is the largest filer of PERM applications, according to data from the US labor department. The company said in a statement that about 80% of the H-1B applications it filed in the last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of current employees, not to hire new workers. In July, the company said it would [USN:L4N4380XC TEXT:"cut 4,800 jobs"], or about 2.1% of its global workforce. Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling said the suspension would also cover Cognizant (CTSH.O) , Infosys (INFY.NS) , Tata Consultancy Services (TCS.NS) , Wipro (WIPR.NS) , HCL Technologies (HCLT.NS) and Capgemini (CAPP.PA) . "We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labor certification applications involving these companies," Sonderling said. He said these companies had since 2009 sought almost three million foreign workers, and had received over 230,000 H-1B visa approvals and over 100,000 permanent labor certifications. Amazon.com was the largest employer of approved H-1B beneficiaries in fiscal 2026, followed by Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, Apple and Microsoft, according to US immigration data. Vance said the suspensions would last "as long as it needs to," adding that the administration wants the companies to change how they hire. He said some companies post ineffective job ads, then cite a lack of applicants to justify hiring lower-paid foreign workers. Microsoft said in its statement that it pays its H-1B employees the same as any other employees doing comparable work. “The immediate financial impact on major technology companies may be relatively limited at this moment, but the longer-term implications for innovation and competitiveness could be much more significant," said Ken Mahoney, CEO of Mahoney Asset Management. Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, HCL Technologies, Wipro and Capgemini did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Tata Consultancy Services declined to comment. Nasscom, India's IT industry body, said Indian tech companies in the US had significantly reduced their reliance on H-1B visas, and relatively few of their workers sought green cards through the PERM process. CRACKDOWN WIDENS The suspensions are the latest in a series of steps against skilled-worker programs. In September last year, the Labor Department launched an enforcement drive called "Project Firewall" as a White House proclamation imposed a one-time $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions for workers hired from abroad. During President Donald Trump's second term, companies have faced growing pressure to keep jobs and production in the United States rather than move them overseas. The action comes despite closer ties between the administration and tech leaders, who are lobbying for lighter AI regulation. UNIVERSITIES UNDER SCRUTINY Vance also said nine universities, including Harvard, Yale and Stanford, would be investigated for what the administration called the misuse of exchange-visitor visas to undercut American wages. The nine schools also include Brown and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Labor Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito said subpoenas had already been served. D'Esposito said investigators would examine whether foreign influence, improper financial relationships or visa abuse were compromising federally funded research. “It could have an enormous economic impact on the whole US economy,” said Sarah Spreitzer, a vice president at the American Council on Education, which represents college and university presidents. International students historically spent $40 billion a year while in the US, she said. The probe deepens the administration's long-running fight with Harvard over foreign students. Last year, the Department of Homeland Security subpoenaed the university over alleged misconduct by international students and its compliance with immigration law. Harvard called that subpoena "unfounded retribution" but said it would comply as far as the law requires.

item.title: Not just a case of déjà vu in France
item.description: Implications of the current nationwide demonstrations over school conditions
item.dc:creator: Mark John
item.content:encoded: Hello. One of the questions that France-watchers inevitably ask as we try to understand the implications of the current nationwide demonstrations over school conditions is: How are they different from the many other street protests that country has seen over the years? As far back as the late 1980s, French schoolchildren were joining often fierce protests over university reform; then in 1995, there were the big public sector strikes over welfare reforms; in the early 2000s, anger once more spilled over onto the streets over then-prime minister Alain Juppé’s attempted pension reform and welfare cuts; nearly two decades later came the “gilets jaunes” and their protests over fuel prices and the rising cost of living. Now, hundreds of thousands of students, parents and teachers are taking to the streets to air longstanding grievances over educational under-funding. Is this, as the French say, just a case of “the more things change, the more they stay the same”? Well, not quite. “In the past, pretty much every time there has been strife, money magically appeared to calm things down,” Paris bureau senior correspondent Leigh Thomas told me of how French governments of the day have so often secured social peace at a price to the state purse. “But there’s not a lot of room to do that now.” This is the problem. Within the politically fraught confines of the French budget debate now taking place, this advanced G7 economy apparently has no money to fix schools where classrooms are [USN:L6N45M0ED TEXT:"infested"] with cockroaches and rats, or where temperatures can swing from freezing to sweltering depending on the weather. This time, things have come to a head with the government hemmed in by investors worried about rising debt in a country which has not balanced its budget since 1974. The yield on French 10-year bonds briefly hit a 24-year high of over 5%, making the cost of its borrowing even higher. The 2027 budget [USN:L1N45N09R TEXT:"presented"] last week by Emmanuel Macron’s government has done little to assuage concerns and anyway is likely to get ripped to shreds in the parliamentary process of the weeks to come. For now, fears that this could balloon into a wider euro zone crisis are probably overdone. For one thing, [USN:L8N45S0RJ TEXT:"the hit"] to French bonds is still nowhere near as big as it was to, say, Italian and Greek debt during the European debt dramas of the 2010s. And while [USN:S8N449067 TEXT:"policymakers"] have made it clear there is no justification at present for the European Central Bank to step in and support French assets, investors broadly sense that the ECB would act if the contagion spread to others. Unless the government can find the extra resources to treat the root causes of the current anger while not further spooking markets, the unhappy stalemate is likely to continue. And this is where the other difference with previous bouts of social strife comes in: the risk it will play well for the political extremes. Whereas in the past, mainstream politicians have been able to just about muddle through, this episode could contribute to their demise. Far-right leader Marine Le Pen was already leading opinion polls ahead of April’s presidential election; the question is whether she will be joined by her far-left rival Jean-Luc Melenchon, a strong supporter of the protests, in the head-to-head second-round runoff. If she is, [USN:L1N44N0WZ TEXT:"surveys"] suggest she will be heading towards the Elysee Palace. France has among the longest life expectancies of any advanced economy, and among the lowest retirement ages: just 63. I think what we're going to be talking about in the labor market is how many tasks are created and destroyed, not how many jobs, because that's AI's impact in the world of work. It's not taking over our jobs, it's taking over our work in certain aspects, giving some of it to the machines and some of it to humans." ADP Chief Economist Nela Richardson.
