item.title: Starbucks has explored Chipotle takeover, FT reports
item.description: Starbucks has explored a takeover of Chipotle Mexican Grill , the Financial Times reported on Thursday, in a move that would reunite Chief Executive Brian Niccol with the burrito chain he led before joining the coffee giant two years ago.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Starbucks (SBUX.O) has explored a takeover of Chipotle Mexican Grill (CMG.N) , the Financial Times reported on Thursday, in a move that would reunite Chief Executive Brian Niccol with the burrito chain he led before joining the coffee giant two years ago. The potential deal comes as restaurant chains wrestle with uncertain demand from inflation-weary consumers and rising operating costs, prompting companies to look for new avenues of growth while facing pressure to improve profitability. Starbucks has worked with advisers in recent months on a takeover proposal for Chipotle, the FT reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Starbucks declined to comment on the report, other than to say it is focused on its turnaround under Niccol, a spokesperson told Reuters. Chipotle did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment. Shares of Chipotle, which has a market capitalization of nearly $39 billion, were up about 6% on Thursday, while those of Starbucks were down about 3%. Starbucks is worth about $107 billion, according to LSEG data. Analysts said any acquisition would likely be a costly undertaking for Starbucks, which is still investing heavily in its turnaround efforts. "A deal could require heavy borrowing or issuing shares," said Lale Akoner, global market strategist at eToro. "Without a compelling financial case, investors may view the deal as an expensive distraction." Starbucks is in the midst of a turnaround under Niccol, who has prioritized customer satisfaction through investments in staffing and store improvements aimed at reducing wait times and restoring the coffeehouse atmosphere that helped make the chain a global brand. [USN:L6N44V1E6 TEXT:"Since joining the company in September 2024, "]Starbucks has committed at least $500 million to labor investments as part of its reorganization, contributing to pressure on profitability. As of the fiscal third quarter, adjusted operating margin was 14.4%, down from 16.7% in the same quarter two years earlier, according to LSEG data. Starbucks has reported four consecutive quarters of comparable sales growth under Niccol, but [USN:L6N43V1FM TEXT:"in July"] he said that "We have more work to do." "The timing of this would be a little weird, given that Starbucks is in the middle of their transformation and hasn't yet shown the margin improvement investors are probably hoping for. Instead of jump-starting the transformation, at first blush, this seems more like jumping the shark instead," said Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management. Chipotle, meanwhile, has been contending with softer traffic as consumers pull back on discretionary spending, while higher food and labor costs have pressured margins across the restaurant industry. Its shares have nearly halved since Niccol left the company. A potential deal could accelerate Chipotle's international expansion, some analysts said. "What I like about this potential is the opportunity CEO Brian Niccol would have to leverage Starbucks' licensed partnerships in Europe to expand Chipotle more aggressively," said Jim Sanderson, an analyst at Northcoast Research. As of the end of last year, Chipotle had nearly 4,000 restaurants in the United States and about 100 international locations. Starbucks, meanwhile, has roughly 40,000 stores globally, including about 18,000 in North America. Niccol joined Starbucks in 2024 after spending six years at Chipotle, where he was credited with steering the company through the aftermath of its food-safety crises and building out its digital business, helping drive years of strong sales growth.

item.title: AkzoNobel, Axalta set to win EU antitrust nod for $25 billion deal, sources say
item.description: Dulux paint maker AkzoNobel and US peer Axalta Coating Systems are set to win EU antitrust approval for their $25 billion merger with a pledge to sell AkzoNobel's vehicle refinish business to address competition concerns, people familiar with the matter said.
item.dc:creator: Yun Chee Foo
item.content:encoded: Dulux paint maker AkzoNobel (AKZO.AS) and US peer Axalta Coating Systems (AXTA.N) are set to win EU antitrust approval for their $25 billion merger with a pledge to sell AkzoNobel's vehicle refinish business to address competition concerns, people familiar with the matter said. The companies [USN:L8N3WU04N TEXT:"announced the deal"] in November last year, underscoring a wave of consolidation among paint makers to save money in the face of rising costs and amid uncertainties created by US President Donald Trump's tariffs. The European Commission, which is the EU competition enforcer, AkzoNobel and Axalta declined to comment. The companies, which met with the EU watchdog on Wednesday to discuss the deal and possible remedies, will put in their offer next week. This will then extend the current Commission's October 22 deadline by 10 working days. The EU regulator is expected to clear the deal after its preliminary review, the people said. Earlier concerns about the overlaps in the powder coatings business have been resolved, leaving the vehicle refinish business as the only issue to be addressed, the people said. Axalta exclusively makes coatings, with a strong presence in the US market. Rivals to the companies include BASF's (BASFn.DE) coatings business, Nippon Paint (4612.T) , Sherwin-Williams (SHW.N) and Kansai Nerolac (KANE.NS) .

item.title: Dozens protest in Tokyo after Marine accused of murder in Okinawa
item.description: Dozens of protesters lined up in front of Japan's Foreign Ministry on Thursday after a US Marine was accused of killing a woman in the southernmost prefecture of Okinawa, many holding signs decrying crimes by US service members.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Dozens of protesters lined up in front of Japan's Foreign Ministry on Thursday after a US Marine was accused of [USN:L1N45T08D TEXT:"killing a woman in the southernmost prefecture of Okinawa"], many holding signs decrying crimes by US service members. The case is the latest in a string of incidents stretching back years that have fuelled unease over the large US troop presence on the island chain near Taiwan and China, with US officials warning it could undermine ties vital to security in East Asia. Public reaction to Anna Yagi's killing, however, has been muted compared with the mass demonstrations that followed the rape of a 12-year-old Okinawan girl by three US servicemen in 1995. Lance Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, is suspected of killing Yagi, 39, in a hotel in the Okinawan capital of Naha last weekend and taking her wallet and backpack. Ballard denied the allegations, police said. Leaders of Thursday's protest spoke over loudspeakers about abuses by US service members and called on the government to respond, with others in the crowd rattling noisemakers in assent. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has called the killing "extremely brutal and heinous", and Tokyo said it had strongly protested to the US and demanded measures to prevent a repeat of such incidents. Japan hosts the largest overseas contingent of US forces globally. Most of the 18,000 Japan-based Marines are stationed in Okinawa, which the US held from the end of World War Two until 1972. That presence has repeatedly stirred resentment among residents over issues such as noise, aircraft crashes and the conduct of personnel. The US on Wednesday began a 48-hour pause of military operations and a ban on alcohol while troops undergo training on standards and discipline. Service members have also been given a month-long curfew for a "period of reflection".

item.title: Securitize launches blockchain-based stocks
item.description: Digital asset company Securitize is launching blockchain-based tokenized stock trading in major listed companies like Apple, Nvidia and Microsoft, with tokens backed by underlying shares, the company said on Thursday.
item.dc:creator: Hannah Lang
item.content:encoded: Digital asset company Securitize (SECZ.N) is launching blockchain-based tokenized stock trading in major listed companies like Apple, Nvidia and Microsoft, with tokens backed by underlying shares, the company said on Thursday. Securitize will initially launch its tokenized stocks on the solana blockchain. The company said it expects its tokenized stocks will also trade on NYSE's forthcoming round-the-clock trading venue, as well as a planned trading venue developed by crypto exchange OKX and Intercontinental Exchange. Securitize Stocks preserve investor rights and economic benefits associated with owning a company's shares, Securitize said. The stock products will be available to eligible investors in the US, European Union and other permitted jurisdictions. Securitize Stocks will initially be available to trade during extended trading hours, with plans to offer 24/7 availability in the future. The crypto industry says tokenizing securities [USN:L4N3T81FC TEXT:"could revolutionize markets"] by allowing shares to be traded 24/7 and settled instantly, boosting liquidity and reducing transaction costs. Although [USN:L6N3UW0SJ TEXT:"many tokenized stock products overseas"] are marketed like stocks, they rarely offer the same rights, disclosures and protections as traditional equities.

item.title: Un avión resulta dañado en el aeropuerto de Riad por ataques hutíes, dicen fuentes
item.description: Los hutíes de Yemen, alineados con Irán, intensificaron su letal campaña de ataques contra Arabia Saudita, con el objetivo de bloquear el espacio aéreo y las instalaciones petroleras del reino mediante lanzamientos de misiles que han causado la muerte de tres personas esta semana y han dejado un avión gravemente dañado.
item.dc:creator: Timour Azhari, Federico Maccioni
item.content:encoded: Los hutíes de Yemen, alineados con Irán, intensificaron su letal campaña de ataques contra Arabia Saudita, con el objetivo de bloquear el espacio aéreo y las instalaciones petroleras del reino mediante lanzamientos de misiles que han causado la muerte de tres personas esta semana y han dejado un avión gravemente dañado. El grupo dijo que había atacado el aeropuerto de Riad y advirtió a los trabajadores de que se mantuvieran alejados de las centrales energéticas, que serían objeto de ataques. La metralla procedente de una interceptación o del impacto de otro proyectil había dejado gravemente dañado el avión comercial perteneciente a la aerolínea estatal saudita Saudia Airlines tras incendiarse mientras estaba estacionado en una terminal del aeropuerto el jueves, dijeron tres personas informadas sobre el asunto. Las fuentes dijeron que, según se cree, no había pasajeros a bordo del avión en ese momento, pero no pudieron descartar que haya habido heridos como consecuencia del incidente. En un vídeo verificado por Reuters se veía una espesa columna negra de humo y llamas elevándose desde el aeropuerto de Riad. La oficina de prensa del Gobierno de Arabia Saudita, su autoridad de aviación civil y Saudia Airlines no respondieron a las solicitudes de comentarios enviadas por correo electrónico. Lufthansa y Air India anunciaron que suspendían los vuelos a Riad tras los ataques de los hutíes. Por otra parte, las autoridades sauditas dijeron que los restos de un misil interceptado habían impactado en una guardería y un complejo médico de Riad. Los hutíes afirman que están atacando al reino por su apoyo a las fuerzas gubernamentales en la reavivada guerra civil de Yemen. Arabia Saudita ha dicho que respalda una ofensiva del Gobierno yemení reconocido por la ONU para recuperar territorio de manos de los hutíes. El conflicto, que ahora se ha convertido en una extensión de la guerra entre Estados Unidos e Irán, ha añadido un nuevo caos a una región ya en llamas y amenaza con arrastrar a otros Estados a una agotadora lucha en las montañas, mientras Siria se plantea ahora desplegar tropas para ayudar a Arabia Saudita.

item.title: Thousands of Spaniards march to mark death of octogenarian at heart of housing protests
item.description: Thousands of Spaniards marched through central Madrid on Thursday to mark the death of the 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her home ignited protests across the country and led to a snap election next month.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Thousands of Spaniards marched through central Madrid on Thursday to mark the death of the 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her home ignited protests across the country and led to a snap election next month. Maricarmen Abascal, who died on Wednesday, had been hospitalised for severe anxiety and exhaustion since her [USN:L8N45F0PQ TEXT:" eviction"] on September 23. No cause of death has been announced. Protests over home shortages and surging rents following her eviction prompted Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to call a snap [USN:L8N45R05N TEXT:"general election"] for November 29 after parliament rejected his government's proposals to address a mounting housing crisis. As the sun set in Madrid, thousands followed a line of Tenants Union members, dressed in orange vests and walking arm-in-arm, as they carried a wreath of flowers from a protest camp in central Puerta del Sol square to Abascal's former home near Retiro Park. "They're not deaths; they're murders," the protesters chanted. Several people who received eviction orders have died by suicide in Spain in recent months. Political leaders on Thursday traded blame and invoked Abascal's case in attacks on opponents. Left-leaning parties criticised conservatives who [USN:L1N45O0BD TEXT:"rejected"] legislation in parliament aimed at curbing soaring rental prices. Right-wingers said the leftist central government had been unable to tackle the crisis after eight years in power. Alberto Nuñez Feijoo, leader of the conservative opposition People's Party (PP), accused Sanchez and the Socialists of trying to exploit the housing crisis for political gain before the election. "We will not allow this attempt to manipulate the emotions of the Spanish people; all of this has happened during their eight years in government. It won’t fly," Feijoo said. In the Madrid regional assembly, opposition leader Manuela Bergerot of the leftist Mas Madrid party said Maricarmen — as she has become known across Spain — had died because of "miserable people who put gain above a person's life." She said the last thing Madrid regional leader Isabel Diaz Ayuso had done while Maricarmen was alive was "laugh at her" — a reference to Ayuso's quip on September 28: "At what age do I get to stop paying my landlords? Let me know." Ayuso blamed Sanchez, saying Maricarmen had been evicted under his government. PROTESTERS BLAME 'GREEDY' LANDLORDS News of the octogenarian's death enraged protesters camped on squares in Spain's main cities who chanted that she had been "murdered" because of the greed of her landlords. After an investment fund purchased the building where she had lived for more than 70 years, Abascal lost a lengthy legal battle against rent increases far beyond her pension income, leading to her eviction. While in hospital, she reached a deal to regain her home but she died before she could return. "When everything is private, we will be deprived of everything," said a placard on Puerta del Sol square, where mourners lit candles and left flowers honouring Maricarmen. Outside Abascal's building, mourners left flowers, candles, handwritten notes and children's drawings. "Maricarmen was the straw that broke the camel's back... (she was) a symbol of resistance and unity," said Alex Marinero, a 21-year-old protester. Tributes to Abascal in the Madrid region's legislature also caused arguments as lawmakers accused each other of cynically exploiting the case. The PP, which has absolute majorities in the Madrid regional and local assemblies, refused to hold a minute of silence honouring her. Instead, hard-left deputies staged one outside City Hall and gave Abascal a 60-second standing ovation during a tense debate in the regional assembly, while PP lawmakers remained seated with folded arms. A survey carried out in June and published by state pollster CIS on Thursday found 76.3% of Spaniards supported intervention in the market to guarantee access to housing, while 79% believe the right to housing should take precedence over treating homes as a market commodity. Ombudsman Angel Gabilondo said addressing the housing crisis would require greater commitment from all levels of government. He said his office was preparing a housing report and reiterated proposals including expanding public housing, restricting tourist rentals, increasing rent assistance and strengthening protections against evictions for vulnerable households.

item.title: Man City head to Anfield under cloud of financial rules verdict
item.description: The Premier League resumes this weekend with one of its flagship fixtures, but Manchester City's trip to Liverpool will unfold amid a hostile atmosphere and beneath an unprecedented cloud following the club's guilty verdict in a landmark financial case.
item.dc:creator: Lori Ewing
item.content:encoded: The Premier League resumes this weekend with one of its flagship fixtures, but Manchester City's trip to Liverpool will unfold amid a hostile atmosphere and beneath an unprecedented cloud following the club's guilty verdict in a landmark financial case. City head to Anfield on Sunday for their first league game since an independent commission found the club [USN:L6N45L10G TEXT:"guilty"] of more than 100 serious breaches of the league's financial rules over nine years, as well as charges relating to their failure to co-operate with the investigation. City have [USN:L6N45O0MF TEXT:"appealed"] the decision and continue to maintain their innocence, saying the commission's opinion contains "clear material errors" and that they possess evidence supporting their position. For now, however, the legal battle and the football season occupy the same uneasy space. City have carried on imperiously on the pitch, winning all five of their league matches to start the campaign, and will arrive at Anfield looking to preserve that perfect record. "The feeling is fantastic, to be honest," Maresca told City's in-house media on Thursday. "The players are excited for the next two games (they host Paris St Germain in the Champions League on Wednesday), but especially they are excited because in this moment, we are top of the league, so the players they are just focused on that. "They know that what we can control is the football side. They know they are professionals. They know that the noise is there, but they don't care too much about the noise. They are just focused on this moment, how we can beat Liverpool, how we can, together with the fans, try to win at Anfield." Liverpool, meanwhile, have endured a less convincing opening, with two wins and three draws from their opening five league games. That would normally provide more than enough intrigue for a fixture between two clubs that have shaped much of the top flight's recent history, but events away from the pitch have transformed Sunday's game into something far bigger. "If they want an understanding of how angry the game is going to be, then Anfield will tell them like you would never believe," former Manchester United captain and England defender Gary Neville declared recently on The Overlap podcast. "I suspect there may be banners, there will certainly be chanting. There will be a reception like you have never seen for them at Anfield... it will be a brutal day." SANCTIONS YET TO BE DETERMINED Every City appearance now comes with questions over what ultimately awaits the club, with the appeal process still to run and sanctions yet to be determined. The uncertainty has already prompted discussion over possible compensation claims from opposing teams and players and the broader consequences for English football. Anfield is hardly the gentlest place for City to return to domestic action after the international break. The rivalry between the clubs already carried plenty of edge after years of battles near the top of English football. Now Sunday's encounter will provide the first indication of how City's players handle the scrutiny generated by a verdict that reaches far beyond the usual rhythms of a title race. There is plenty at stake for sixth-placed Liverpool, too. Victory would provide an emphatic lift after their modest start and land the first blow on a City team who have so far been flawless. Defending champions Arsenal, who trail City by three points in second, kick off the weekend at home to Leeds United on Saturday. Mikel Arteta's side know victory would lift them provisionally level on points with Enzo Maresca's City. Leeds have provided one of the season's early surprises, sitting fifth after going unbeaten through five games. Another heavyweight fixture follows later on Saturday when Manchester United host Tottenham Hotspur, with both struggling sides desperate to inject some momentum into their seasons. United are 12th with just one victory, while Spurs are bottom with just two points. The meeting adds another layer of intrigue to a weekend already dominated by events at Anfield, with two traditional powers under pressure to turn around difficult starts when they meet at Old Trafford. Yet inevitably most eyes will be fixed on Anfield. After an unusually long pause in domestic football, the Premier League returns with its most contentious off-field controversy far from resolved.

item.title: Nvidia-backed Iambic Therapeutics launches IPO as biotechs buck market gloom
item.description: Nvidia-backed Iambic Therapeutics, which uses AI to develop drugs, is aiming to raise up to $159.4 million in its US IPO, as the biotech sector emerges as a bright spot in an otherwise lackluster market.
item.dc:creator: Manya Saini, Niket Nishant
item.content:encoded: Nvidia-backed Iambic Therapeutics, which uses AI to develop drugs, is aiming to raise up to $159.4 million in its US IPO, as the biotech sector emerges as a bright spot in an otherwise lackluster market. The initial public offering would value the drugmaker at up to $805.8 million — towards the top of its indicated price range — based on the number of outstanding shares listed in its prospectus, a regulatory filing showed on Tuesday. AI-driven drug discovery is among the few areas where the technology's promise is translating into growing investor interest, as biotech companies use it to identify drug candidates and speed up parts of the development process. Iambic is marketing roughly 9.38 million shares at $15 to $17 apiece. Investment firms ARK Investment Management and Duquesne Family Office have indicated interest in purchasing shares worth $60 million. Founded in 2019 as Entos, Iambic is advancing a pipeline of drug candidates developed using its AI platform to treat solid tumors. It has partnerships with some top pharma companies, including AbbVie (ABBV.N) and Takeda Pharmaceutical (4502.T) . "I would characterize it as a clinical-stage biotech company with an AI-enhanced drug discovery platform, rather than a pure AI play," said Kat Liu, vice president at IPOX. The valuation depends primarily on pipeline strength and the probability of eventual approval and commercialization, Liu added. A successful listing would set Iambic apart in a [USN:L4N45L0SK TEXT:"fall IPO market hit"] by a string of delays as rising Treasury yields and market volatility make investors more cautious. Concerns over an overheating AI trade and persistent geopolitical tensions have further dampened appetite, [USN:L4N45H0ML TEXT:"leaving biotech"] among the few areas still drawing interest. Iambic is aiming to trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "IAM" after the offering. J.P.Morgan, Jefferies, BofA Securities and Citigroup are the lead underwriters.

item.title: Dólar baja cae a medida que los rendimientos de bonos europeos descienden desde máximos
item.description: El dólar bajó el jueves ya que se moderó la subida de los rendimientos de los bonos de la zona euro, mientras que las expectativas sobre la trayectoria de las tasas de interés de la Reserva Federal para este año se mantenían prácticamente intactas.
item.dc:creator: Chuck Mikolajczak
item.content:encoded: El dólar bajó el jueves ya que se moderó la subida de los rendimientos de los bonos de la zona euro, mientras que las expectativas sobre la trayectoria de las tasas de interés de la Reserva Federal para este año se mantenían prácticamente intactas. Los rendimientos gubernamentales en la zona del euro volvieron a subir con fuerza, ya que el repunte de los precios del petróleo intensificó el temor a la inflación, y los inversionistas siguieron vendiendo bonos de países muy endeudados, como Francia e Italia. Sin embargo, el euro se recuperó de sus mínimos anteriores tras un retroceso de los rendimientos. El retorno francés a 10 años ganó 2 puntos básicos al 4,8873%, tras haber alcanzado un máximo del 4,9685% durante la jornada. Francia se ha visto especialmente afectada, ya que los inversionistas analizan minuciosamente su nivel de deuda, su déficit presupuestario y sus perspectivas políticas antes de las elecciones presidenciales de 2027. En España, los sindicatos anunciaron este miércoles una huelga general por cuestiones de vivienda para el 11 de noviembre, una protesta que tendrá lugar unas semanas antes de las elecciones anticipadas. Mientras, las expectativas de una subida de tasas de la Fed en su reunión de política monetaria a finales de este mes siguen siendo bajas, después de que las minutas publicadas el miércoles de la última reunión del banco central mostraron que los responsables consideraban la inflación como el mayor riesgo para sus perspectivas, y los analistas señalaron que no ofrecían sorpresas. El gobernador de la Fed Christopher Waller dijo el jueves que probablemente serán necesarias más subidas de las tasas de interés para reducir la inflación hasta el objetivo del 2%, pero añadió que existía "flexibilidad" en cuanto al ritmo de alzas y dejó la puerta abierta a una pausa en la próxima reunión en octubre. El índice dólar , que mide el valor del billete verde frente a una cesta de divisas, cayó un 0,08%, a 102,17, tras haber subido hasta 102,46, mientras que el euro avanzó un 0,08%, a 1,1204 dólares, tras haber descendido a 1,1171 dólares durante la jornada. La libra esterlina sumó un 0,07%, a 1,3219 dólares, después de que el gobernador del Banco de Inglaterra, Andrew Bailey, dijo que los Gobiernos deben redoblar sus esfuerzos para demostrar que pueden sanear sus finanzas públicas, ya que los mercados de bonos de todo el mundo están sintiendo la presión de los altos niveles de endeudamiento y las crecientes presiones inflacionistas. Frente al yen japonés , el dólar se debilitó un 0,12%, a 157,88.

item.title: Venture Global breached LNG supply deal with Galp, tribunal rules
item.description: Venture Global said on Thursday an arbitration tribunal found its Calcasieu Pass unit breached an LNG supply agreement with Portugal's Galp , marking the second setback for the firm over cargo deliveries from the project.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Venture Global (VG.N) said on Thursday an arbitration tribunal found its Calcasieu Pass unit breached an LNG supply agreement with Portugal's Galp (GALP.LS) , marking the second setback for the firm over cargo deliveries from the project. BP (BP.L) is the only other company to have prevailed in arbitration proceedings against Venture Global, as the US exporter dealt with a string of disputes with long-term LNG buyers, which also included Shell (SHEL.L) , Repsol (REP.MC) , Italy's Edison (EDNn.MI) and Poland's Orlen (PKN.WA) . Venture Global faces potential damages of billions of dollars from the disputes. The company has argued the spot sales were permitted, but two arbitration panels have now disagreed. Venture Global won its arbitration cases brought by [USN:L1N3U4117 TEXT:"Shell"] and [USN:L6N3YM1DM TEXT:"Repsol"], and subsequently defeated a court challenge related to the Shell arbitration award. It [USN:L4N40E1PP TEXT:"settled"] with Italy's Edison earlier this year, with Venture Global agreeing to supply additional LNG cargoes beyond those required under their long-term contract. Its only outstanding arbitration is with Poland's Orlen (PKN.WA) , which is expected to be resolved by the end of the year. The buyers accused Venture Global of selling cargoes on the spot market at higher prices following Russia's invasion of Ukraine instead of delivering contracted volumes from initial production at the Louisiana plant. Venture Global argued the spot sales were allowed as faulty power-island equipment delayed the start of commercial operations. Galp said in an emailed statement that it was reviewing the tribunal's decision and assessing next steps. The amount of money Venture Global will have to pay to Galp will be determined in a separate damages hearing expected in 2027 or 2028, with any final award not exceeding $170 million under the seller aggregate cap agreement, Venture Global said in its regulatory filing on Thursday. Capital One said in a note on Thursday that it views the $170 million liability cap as "relatively immaterial." Venture Global shares were up more than 2% at $13.34 at midday on Thursday. Venture Global added that one of the three arbitrators at the International Chamber of Commerce tribunal dissented and that it is evaluating its options while continuing to defend its position. The company also said the ruling does not affect the agreement currently being performed by the parties and noted it has delivered 20 cargoes to Galp since Calcasieu Pass reached commercial operations. After BP [USN:L3N3VQ1G3 TEXT:"won"] its arbitration case in 2025, Venture Global said in its annual report that the British firm is seeking at least $3.7 billion in damages, though the claim could exceed $6 billion before interest, costs and fees.

item.title: Euro zone ministers tell France to pass 2027 budget to calm markets
item.description: Euro zone finance ministers and the European Central Bank told France on Thursday to pass a 2027 budget to calm bond markets, as French borrowing costs hover at 25-year highs.
item.dc:creator: Jan Strupczewski
item.content:encoded: Euro zone finance ministers and the European Central Bank told France on Thursday to pass a 2027 budget to calm bond markets, as French borrowing costs hover at 25-year highs. Euro zone finance ministers and the ECB meet in Luxembourg on Thursday afternoon for monthly talks and the surge in French borrowing costs was discussed. France is at the centre of a bond market storm on worries over the country’s large budget deficit and looming 2027 presidential election. Its 10-year bond yield has jumped nearly 80 basis points (bps) since the start of September and hit its highest level since July 2002, just short of 5%. That is driving up borrowing costs and making the fiscal maths harder. "It is essential that all member states, and in particular those with high deficits or debts, implement prudent fiscal policies," EU Economic Commissioner Dombrovskis, who took part in the ministerial talks, told a news conference afterwards. "Putting in place a sound budget for the next year will be important to ensure this predictability and credibility and to reassure markets. I'm in contact with,(French Finance) Minister Lescure on this," he said. France said in September that its budget deficit will overshoot the government's 5% target this year. The government has announced tightening measures to bring some calm, but investors are sceptical they can be carried out because of the fragmentation of the French parliament and presidential and parliamentary elections in April and May 2027. France also plans to sell a record €340 billion ($381 billion) of bonds in 2027 to fund the government and refinance COVID-era debt. "We have confidence in France's commitment vis-a-vis public finances," the chairman of euro zone finance ministers Kyriakos Pierrakakis told the news conference. Officials said no euro zone institution was ready to jump in to help France lower its borrowing costs. Officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, made clear it was up to French politicians to sort out the uncertainty they have created. The European Central Bank can buy bonds of a euro zone country on the secondary market, if their prices move in an unjustified way, to protect the transmission of monetary policy. ECB President Christine Lagarde told euro zone ministers the central bank had instruments to counter unwarranted, disorderly market dynamics that threaten the smooth transmission of monetary policy, but they were subject to clear eligibility criteria, according to officials familiar with the discussions. Published on the ECB website, the criteria include compliance with the EU's fiscal rules and not being in an EU excessive deficit procedure -- disciplinary action for countries with budget deficits higher than the EU ceiling of 3% of GDP. France is in such a disciplinary process with a budget gap above 5% of GDP. Its fiscal policies do not match the fiscal consolidation path agreed with the EU, so it would not be eligible for ECB help. Since the creation of the euro currency in 1999, France -- the European Union's second biggest economy and a key political player -- has only had a budget deficit below the EU's ceiling of 3% six times. Some officials said that debt markets were probably the only factor that could force it to consolidate.

item.title: Moroccan defense firm MMI targets turret deliveries in March 2027
item.description: Defense firm Moroccan Military Industry (MMI) will begin delivering armoured vehicle turrets to the Moroccan army in March 2027, its general manager said, as Rabat pushes to build up its military industry with foreign partners.
item.dc:creator: Ahmed Eljechtimi
item.content:encoded: Defense firm Moroccan Military Industry (MMI) will begin delivering armoured vehicle turrets to the Moroccan army in March 2027, its general manager said, as Rabat pushes to build up its military industry with foreign partners. MMI has a weapons systems facility in the Midparc industrial zone near Casablanca, while a second plant in Sidi Yahya, north of Rabat, is being established to manufacture medium and large-calibre ammunition, General Manager Kaduri Naor told Reuters on the sidelines of the Marrakech Air Show. Sources at the air show and earlier media reports have said MMI is closely linked to Israeli defense company Elbit Systems and uses its technology. MMI told Reuters it is a Moroccan defense company. Morocco and Israel resumed diplomatic ties in 2020 and signed a defense cooperation pact in 2021, opening the way for collaboration in air defense, artillery, drones and defense manufacturing. MMI has agreed with Morocco's defense administration to produce the turrets to be installed on 8x8 armoured vehicles assembled in Morocco by India's Tata, as well as related ammunition, Naor said. MMI is developing an anti-drone version of the same turret, targeting a rapidly growing global market as militaries seek lower-cost defenses against unmanned aerial threats, he said. "The threat is very cheap... defense systems are more expensive," he said, adding that MMI's solution was "cost-effective". The ammunition for the anti-drone turret will be produced in Morocco, equipped with a small radar that is designed to sense an incoming drone and trigger an explosion, dispersing tungsten fragments to destroy the target, he said. MMI is also planning to produce a self-propelled mortar system that can be mounted on vehicles, he said. The company hopes to use Morocco as a platform for exports, Naor said. "We will have a European NATO country to export to," he said, declining to identify the customer. Naor said 99% of MMI's staff, including engineers, were Moroccan.

item.title: Wall St turns lower as crude spikes, chip stocks weigh
item.description: Wall Street dipped on Thursday as crude prices surged on a spike in Middle East tensions and a cut in US output that fed inflation and rate-hike fears, while semiconductor stocks slumped.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Culp, Tharuniyaa Lakshmi
item.content:encoded: Wall Street dipped on Thursday as crude prices surged on a spike in Middle East tensions and a cut in US output that fed inflation and rate-hike fears, while semiconductor stocks slumped. All three major US stock indexes lost ground, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq down the most. Chipmakers (.SOX) , which have soared over 80% so far this year, were clear underperformers, falling 3.0%. Investors worried that rising interest rates could become a headwind to the rapid AI buildout, which has leaned heavily on debt for funding. "The market is in a state of nervousness due to high oil prices, as it prepares for earnings season which basically starts next week," said Peter Cardillo, chief market economist at Spartan Capital Securities in New York. "That's the excuse for what I believe is profit-taking." "It's a somewhat cautious market, but 'cautious' is not a dirty word," Cardillo added. [USN:L1N45U031 TEXT:"Oil prices"] jumped on supply concerns after a spate of attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, combined with a cut in US output due to hurricane activity. Tight global crude supplies during the Iran war have sent US crude soaring more than 60% so far this year, stoking inflation pressures. In response to those pressures, the US Federal Reserve hiked interest rates in September for the first time since July 2023. During Thursday's session, benchmark US Treasury yields inched higher, hovering near multi-year highs, while yields on 2-year notes, which tend to reflect Fed rate expectations, moved up more decisively. Financial markets currently expect the central bank to leave rates unchanged this month, while the probability of a December hike is currently at 67.9%, according to CME's FedWatch tool. That mirrors the expected rate hike path of the [USN:L6N45U0QU TEXT:"European Central Bank"], and was affirmed by Fed Governor [USN:L6N45T15S TEXT:"Christopher Waller"], who said additional rate hikes will probably be necessary, but the timing of those hikes is "flexible." The Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) fell 34.69 points, or 0.07%, to 51,145.18, the S&P 500 (.SPX) lost 47.95 points, or 0.61%, to 7,753.82 and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) lost 378.50 points, or 1.37%, to 27,160.19. Among the 11 major sectors in the S&P 500, energy stocks (.SPNY) led the percentage gainers, while technology (.SPLRCT) , weighed by chips, suffered the steepest loss. Memory-chip giant Samsung Electronics' (005930.KS) record quarterly profit forecast failed to lift sentiment, with its shares closing lower in South Korea. Rival Micron Technology (MU.O) dropped 4.1%. On Wednesday, the Wall Street Journal reported that [USN:FWN45T25Y TEXT:"Broadcom"] (AVGO.O) is lining up $50 billion in financing for OpenAI, with Oracle (ORCL.N) also seeking an unspecified sum, spurring fears that massive debt issuance by technology companies could intensify the competition for capital. Broadcom fell 3.9% and Oracle fell 4.9%. [USN:L6N45U0N9 TEXT:"PepsiCo"] (PEP.O) shares gained 2.1% after the beverage company said it would pursue additional spending cuts while lowering its annual core profit forecast. [USN:L6N45U0YO TEXT:"Starbucks"] (SBUX.O) dipped 4.2% following reports that the coffee chain was exploring a purchase of Chipotle Mexican Grill (CMG.N) , whose shares jumped 7.3%. Palantir (PLTR.O) climbed 1.6% after Goldman Sachs upgraded its rating on the data analytics software provider to "buy" from "neutral". Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.07-to-1 ratio on the NYSE. There were 83 new highs and 392 new lows on the NYSE. On the Nasdaq, 1,882 stocks rose and 2,815 fell as declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.5-to-1 ratio. The S&P 500 posted four new 52-week highs and 12 new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 24 new highs and 285 new lows.

item.title: UK watchdog proposes 90-day redemption notice period for illiquid assets
item.description: Britain's finance watchdog on Thursday proposed that investors holding illiquid assets such as property must give 90 days' notice to their asset managers to withdraw money, in a move designed to reduce the risk of rushed asset sales that can harm markets.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Britain's finance watchdog on Thursday proposed that investors holding illiquid assets such as property must give 90 days' notice to their asset managers to withdraw money, in a move designed to reduce the risk of rushed asset sales that can harm markets. The Financial Conduct Authority said the new notice period would give fund managers time to sell assets in an orderly way, making liquidity-driven suspensions less likely Existing funds would have two years to comply and will have to give investors at least one year’s notice, the regulator said The new rules are intended to strengthen liquidity risk management and help funds meet redemption requests in line with their terms, while protecting remaining investors and supporting market integrity, the FCA added It said the proposal brings the UK in line with new international liquidity standards for open-ended funds

item.title: Data centers' 'flexible' power usage could save the grid billions. Can they scale?
item.description: Technology companies and utilities are increasingly exploring ways to make power-hungry data centers more flexible in when and how they consume electricity, helping ease the strain on US power grids as AI-driven demand surges.
item.dc:creator: Kavya Balaraman
item.content:encoded: Technology companies and utilities are increasingly exploring ways to make power-hungry data centers more flexible in when and how they consume electricity, helping ease the strain on US power grids as AI-driven demand surges. The strategy, called "demand response", involves data centers temporarily reducing or shifting electricity use during periods of peak demand or grid stress, and is gaining traction as a way to reduce the need for costly grid upgrades and new power generation. It's a tool that states around the US, federal agencies and market operators are increasingly exploring, said Lauren Shwisberg, a principal at energy think tank RMI. WHY DOES DATA CENTER FLEXIBILITY MATTER? US data center electricity use could rise from about 177 to 192 terawatt-hours in 2024 to between 383 and 793 TWh by 2030, according to the Electric Power Research Institute. Meanwhile, data centers surveyed by the group reported peak power reduction potential of 10% to 30%, depending on facility type, with some hyperscalers going even higher, according to Arin Kaye, EPRI technical leader. A study by Duke University's Nicholas Institute estimated that greater flexibility from data centers could save between $40 billion and $150 billion in capital investments over the next decade. It could also help data centers connect to the grid more quickly, as regulators and grid operators explore faster pathways for facilities willing to curb electricity use during periods of high demand. WHERE DO EFFORTS STAND? So far, the "demand response" strategy for data centers has mostly been deployed through pilot projects or one-off agreements. OpenAI, for example, recently agreed to cut the electricity it draws from the grid by up to 1 gigawatt from a planned 3.2-gigawatt facility in Georgia during periods of grid stress. This, however, is gradually evolving into a broader push. Federal regulators in June [USN:L6N42Q13P TEXT:"ordered"] grid operators to consider new rules for connecting large power users to the grid, including new pathways for facilities offering this flexibility to connect faster. Last month, Alphabet's (GOOGL.O) Google, NVIDIA (NVDA.O) and Emerald AI launched an initiative called the AI Energy Management Alliance, aimed at advancing the deployment of "flexible" data centers. WHAT ARE THE KEY CHALLENGES? Experts say scaling up the strategy will require changes on both sides. Data centers need to figure out how to adjust power consumption without disrupting customers, while utilities and grid operators need to develop tariffs, market incentives and faster interconnection pathways that reward that flexibility. "Demand response can materially soften peak impacts, but scaling curtailment agreements across hundreds of new facilities will demand significant capital expenditure and coordinated policy frameworks," said Alexander Kheder, analyst with BMI, a unit of Fitch Solutions.

item.title: Barril sube 5%, pero luego recorta ganancias por comentarios de Trump sobre Irán
item.description: Los precios del petróleo subieron más de un 5 % el jueves, pero luego recortaban ganancias después de que el presidente Donald Trump dijo que Estados Unidos no lanzará un ataque contra Irán antes de las elecciones legislativas de noviembre.
item.dc:creator: Arathy Somasekhar
item.content:encoded: Los precios del petróleo subieron más de un 5 % el jueves, pero luego recortaban ganancias después de que el presidente Donald Trump dijo que Estados Unidos no lanzará un ataque contra Irán antes de las elecciones legislativas de noviembre. Los futuros del crudo Brent subían 3,48 dólares, un 3,5%, a 103,73 dólares el barril, a las 1641 GMT, mientras que el West Texas Intermediate (WTI) subía 2,69 dólares, o un 3,1%, a 91 dólares. En sus máximos de la sesión, ambos contratos subieron más de 5 dólares por barril, con el Brent en su nivel más alto desde el 29 de septiembre debido a la preocupación por ataques inminentes de Estados Unidos contra Irán y a una pérdida de oferta en el Golfo de México a causa del huracán Isaías. Posteriormente, Trump dijo que Washington estaba manteniendo conversaciones productivas con Irán. La agencia de noticias Tasnim informó que el ministro de Asuntos Exteriores, Abbas Araqchi, había declarado que Teherán está analizando la respuesta de Estados Unidos a su propuesta, según la cual el estrecho de Ormuz podría reabrirse en un plazo de siete días, y que podría dar una respuesta en los próximos días. Las amenazas al transporte marítimo de petróleo en el golfo Pérsico y el estrecho de Ormuz —por donde antes de la guerra circulaban envíos equivalentes a alrededor del 20% del crudo y el combustible mundiales— han aumentado en octubre, lo que ha impulsado los precios. Los ataques a petroleros que navegaban por el estrecho la semana pasada alcanzaron su nivel más alto desde que comenzó la guerra. "La frecuencia de los ataques iraníes contra buques se encuentra ahora en su punto más alto desde que comenzó la guerra, y es probable que se intensifique aún más", dijo Saul Kavonic, director de energía de MST Marquee. "Las restricciones en los flujos de productos, los costos logísticos extremos y la alta probabilidad de una escalada por parte de Irán están manteniendo los precios altos".

item.title: Venezuela's Maduro charged in US with ordering torture of opponents, Americans
item.description: US prosecutors on Thursday charged ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores with conspiring to torture political opponents and American citizens, adding to the drug trafficking case the couple already faced.
item.dc:creator: Luc Cohen
item.content:encoded: US prosecutors on Thursday charged ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores with conspiring to torture political opponents and American citizens, adding to the drug trafficking case the couple already faced. Separately, US District Judge [USN:L1N3Y8014 TEXT:"Alvin Hellerstein"], who is overseeing the case, denied a request by Flores to be released from jail due to health concerns ahead of a trial scheduled for next year. Maduro, 63, and Flores, 69, were captured on January 3 in their Caracas home during a US military operation ordered by President Donald Trump , and were flown to New York to face drug charges against them that were announced that same day. A superseding indictment filed in Manhattan federal court on Thursday added the torture count to the existing criminal case. Maduro and Flores each would face a mandatory minimum 50 years in prison if convicted of all the charges. They have [USN:L6N3Y607X TEXT:"pleaded not guilty"] to the original charges, but have not yet entered pleas to the new indictment, which detailed alleged torture against nine people, including three US citizens. In a statement, Maduro's lawyer Barry Pollack said, "President Maduro denies the charges in the new indictment and looks forward to his day in court." Flores' lawyers Mark Donnelly and Andres Sanchez in a statement said their client denies the allegations. They questioned why prosecutors only revealed the indictment, which court records showed was returned under seal by a grand jury on Tuesday, shortly before Thursday's hearing. "We look forward to fully responding to the allegations in court at the appropriate time," Donnelly and Sanchez said. Since Maduro's capture, Venezuela has boosted cooperation with the US under the leadership of his former Vice-President Delcy Rodriguez. Relations between the United States and oil-rich Venezuela were tense during the socialist Maduro's 13 years in power. US officials and human rights groups have long accused Venezuelan officials of torturing detainees, but Thursday's indictment marked the first time Maduro faced criminal charges over the allegations. The indictment alleged that thousands of Venezuelans were threatened, arrested, tortured or killed at the hands of the state between 1999 and 2025. Before Maduro became president in 2013, both he and Flores held positions in the late Venezuelan President Hugo Chavez's government. 'A VIOLENT SYSTEM' "Maduro, Flores and other high-ranking members of their inner circle used a violent system of torture and repression to maintain their power," Jamie McDonald, the top federal prosecutor in Manhattan, told reporters outside the courthouse after Flores' bail was denied. Flores was Venezuela's attorney general and led its National Assembly before becoming first lady. Many of the incidents of alleged torture described in the indictment occurred during times of political unrest in Venezuela or in response to perceived threats against Maduro. In one instance, prosecutors said, Maduro in 2013 ordered the arrest of a Venezuelan military officer he suspected of planning a coup. Members of Venezuela's military counterintelligence directorate then interrogated the officer while shocking the individual with a live electric wire around 20 times and hung the individual by the hands and feet for several minutes at a time, prosecutors said. In 2022, an American citizen detained while entering Venezuela was accused of conspiring to assassinate Maduro and was tortured by military counterintelligence officers through beatings and shocks to the person's arms, legs and genitals, according to the indictment. FLORES DENIED RELEASE Flores' lawyers had argued their client should be released on bail because she needs a cardiac procedure and wants to recover in a more comfortable environment. The lawyers proposed moving her to a residence in the New York City area with round-the-clock private security, and said she is not a danger to the community. In denying the motion for bail, Hellerstein decided the evidence against Flores appeared strong. The judge also said Flores, who wore a dark prison T-shirt and a headset to listen to a simultaneous Spanish translation of the proceedings, appeared to be relatively healthy. "For whatever it's worth, her appearance today is no worse and perhaps a little better than when I first met with her on her arraignment," Hellerstein said, referring to her first appearance in court on January 5. "She was still bandaged up from the military invasion," Donnelly said. Prosecutors in the Manhattan US Attorney's Office opposed Flores' release. They said Flores has received adequate medical care at the detention center, and if released poses an "extreme" risk of flight and danger to the public, including possible witness intimidation. Hellerstein's bail denial will not affect Flores' trial or potential punishment. Maduro and Flores have been held at Brooklyn's Metropolitan Detention Center since their capture. Their trial is scheduled for June 1, 2027.

item.title: Why EV sales are lukewarm in America, but hot in Europe
item.description: US car shoppers have been slow to warm back up to electric vehicles since a key federal subsidy expired a year ago, despite persistently high gas prices, while Europeans have flocked to the cars.
item.dc:creator: Kalea Hall
item.content:encoded: US car shoppers have been slow to warm back up to electric vehicles since a key federal subsidy expired a year ago, despite persistently high gas prices, while Europeans have flocked to the cars. EV sales in the US are down 30.7% this year through September, according to research firm Motor Intelligence, accounting for just 6% of overall sales. That's less than the 8.5% at this time a year ago, when buyers rushed to beat the expiration of a $7,500 federal tax credit. In Europe, however, buyers have flocked to electrics for relief from higher fuel prices stemming from the war in Iran. EVs accounted for 23.2% of the European auto market this year through September, up from 17.7% a year earlier, according to the European Automobile Manufacturers' Association. The divergence in the two markets is due in part to key policy differences between the two regions. In Europe, automakers continue to roll out electric models to meet stringent tailpipe-emissions regulations, and Chinese automakers have stormed the European market with a slew of imported EVs. In the US, the Trump administration worked with Congress to eliminate support for EVs , and watered down fuel-efficiency regulations. High tariffs and a ban on Chinese-made vehicle software have effectively blocked Chinese car brands. Meanwhile, there were more than [USN:L8N45O0IP TEXT:"150 EVs on sale in Europe"] during the first half of 2026, up from about 100 models in 2024, according to Transport & Environment, a Brussels-based environmental advocacy group. Many are priced below 25,000 euros ($27,995), and many countries offer tax breaks to lower consumers’ out-of-pocket costs. US BUYERS GO FOR HYBRIDS, USED EVS Since the expiration of the $7,500 federal tax credit a year ago, many US automakers have discontinued electric models or scrapped plans for new entries. Some have done away with cheap leases that helped fuel demand. Buyers instead are [USN:L6N4570VU TEXT:"seeking hybrids"] and used EVs, car dealers and analysts say. Hybrid sales jumped 23% through the first three quarters from the year-earlier period, accounting for 15.6% of total sales over that stretch. “There's still demand out there [for EVs], but the energy and the masses are definitely running to hybrid technology,” said Thad Szott, a Detroit-area dealer with Ford (F.N) , Stellantis (STLAM.MI) and Toyota (7203.T) . Some automakers are adding hybrids to their showrooms. Nissan, for example, moved up the launch of a new hybrid system on its popular Rogue SUV by several months. Hybrids are “a safer choice” for consumers worried about driving range, said Tiago Castro, Nissan’s senior vice president of US marketing and sales. “When we had the government incentive” for EVs, he said, “it was a different story.” The market for used EVs is bustling, though, a sign that less affluent buyers are seeking relief from high fuel prices. Sales of used electric cars rose 19% through September from the year-earlier period, according to research site CarGurus. TESLA, RIVIAN EVS FARE BETTER THAN LEGACY CARMAKERS EV-only brands have fared better than traditional automakers' EV sales. Tesla’s (TSLA.O) US sales fell only 14% in the first three quarters, a milder decline than the broader electric vehicle market, according to an estimate from Motor Intelligence. Rivian’s (RIVN.O) US sales rose 29%, helped by the release of a new SUV, the R2. By contrast, Ford's EV sales are down 68% this year through September, while crosstown rival General Motors (GM.N) saw a 43% drop in EV sales. Honda has opted to end production of its EVs after this year, while planning to expand hybrid sales. “Once they scaled back the $7,500, it became obvious” that EV market share would decline, said Lance Woelfer, vice president of US auto sales at Honda. However, South Korean automaker Hyundai (005380.KS) has seen some recovery in EV sales since gas prices began rising in late winter, and dealers are asking for them, said Randy Parker, CEO of Hyundai Motor North America. “We're not giving up on EVs by any stretch of the imagination,” Parker said. (1 euro = $1.1197)

item.title: Democrats in tight Midwest US races split on trans rights strategy
item.description: Some are adopting more conservative stances and others are trying to deflect.
item.dc:creator: Helen Coster, Leah Douglas
item.content:encoded: After being caught flat-footed on transgender issues in the last US election, Democrats in tight midterm races are pursuing different strategies, with some adopting more conservative stances and others trying to deflect, according to a Reuters review of campaign messaging and interviews with nine party strategists and insiders. Ahead of the November 3 election, vulnerable Republican candidates have renewed their attacks over transgender rights, a message that political strategists say helped Donald Trump and his party win unified control of Washington in 2024. In response, some Democratic candidates have moved closer to Republican positions on transgender participation in women's sports and gender-affirming care for minors. Others are seeking to redirect the conversation back to the [USN:L6N45N0PD TEXT:"flagging economy"] and Trump’s [USN:L6N44L0VD TEXT:"unpopular war with Iran"]. The different strategies can be seen most clearly in [USN:L6N44F10S TEXT:"Iowa"] and [USN:L6N45916H TEXT:"Ohio"], states that Republicans have dominated during the Trump era but which now feature competitive congressional and gubernatorial races. Whether Democrats in these Midwestern states can convince moderate voters they agree with their views on trans issues, or successfully change the topic, could determine how much support they are able to win back from cultural conservatives — and could foreshadow how the party's presidential hopefuls handle the issue in 2028. Critics warn that moving towards Republicans on trans issues is unlikely to win Democrats new support, and risks alienating LGBTQ voters and the party’s [USN:L6N4431B9 TEXT:"ascendant progressive wing"]. DEMOCRATS MOVE RIGHT In Iowa, Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand, Senate candidate Josh Turek and congressional candidates Lindsay James and Sarah Trone Garriott have all distanced themselves from progressive positions on transgender issues. “I oppose letting men in women's locker rooms and voted to let parents, not politicians, make decisions for their kids,” Trone Garriott said in a recent ad. LGBTQ advocates have criticized such language, saying misgendering transgender women as men represents a betrayal of the party's LGBTQ supporters at a uniquely vulnerable moment. Since returning to office, Trump has directed the federal government to recognize only two sexes; sought to bar transgender people from military service; restricted transgender girls' participation in women's sports, and moved to limit federal support for gender-affirming care for minors. “You don't have to capitulate and use Republican talking points to win elections,” said Aime Wichtendahl, the first transgender person elected to the Iowa General Assembly. Gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand told Politico last month that "girls' sports are for girls." And his approach may be working, with polls showing him favored to become the first Democrat to win the governor's race since 2006. At a recent town hall he said “I tend to agree” with Republicans that transgender women and girls should be barred from female sports teams. “Coward!” a man in the room shouted in protest. 'PARENTS KNOW WHAT'S BEST' Transgender issues have also featured prominently in Ohio, which Trump carried by double digits in 2024. Republican Derek Merrin, running to represent the 9th congressional district, released a September 10 ad saying that Democratic incumbent Marcy Kaptur had “voted to let biological men compete against girls in their sports.” Kaptur, who faces an uphill race in her recently redrawn district, countered a week later with an ad saying she had “voted with Republicans to keep transgender ideology out of our schools because parents know what’s best for their kids … and boys should not play in girls’ sports.” The ad was criticized by local LGBTQ organizations, including the Lucas County Stonewall Democrats, who wrote in a letter to Kaptur that she was “engaged in a race to the bottom with Republicans.” Asked for a response to that letter, Kaptur's campaign did not respond. Former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown, running against Trump-backed Jon Husted, has tried a different approach. A recent ad from Elon Musk’s PAC accused him of supporting an “extremist” agenda under which children are “abused and exploited” through “sex change surgery.” Brown, who polls show with a narrow lead over Husted, has opted not to engage, framing the attacks as a distraction from more pressing issues: “With everything going on, that’s what they’re talking about?” asks one Ohio voter who was featured in a recent ad from Brown’s campaign. THE ISSUE THAT BOXED IN HARRIS Among the most indelible ads from [USN:L1N37143D TEXT:"2024’s presidential contest"] between Trump and former Vice President Kamala Harris was one that featured the tagline: “Kamala is for they/them. President Trump is for you.” A Democratic Party election report concluded the ads were “very effective” and boxed in Harris, who had previously supported gender-affirming care for inmates in federal custody. A [USN:L1N41503A TEXT:"Reuters/Ipsos poll in April"] found that 67% of survey respondents supported banning transgender people from competing in female school sports. But the party splits were severe: Ninety-two percent of Republicans said they supported such bans, compared with just 44% of Democrats. “We have extensive research that shows voters prefer an argument that broadens the conversation to all of us and doesn't leave anyone behind over a divisive narrative that misgenders people and throws them under the bus," said Tyler Hack, executive director of the Christopher Street Project, a transgender advocacy organization. With their anti-trans attacks, Republicans are “abandoning pocketbook issues in favor of an anti-freedom agenda that is obsessed with politicians making decisions that should be left to parents and schools,” Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee spokesperson Viet Shelton said in a statement, echoing a framing used by Republicans that emphasizes local government control on transgender policies. Democratic strategist Eric Stern thinks Republicans got “over-confident” about the effectiveness of their anti-trans strategy in 2024. “I’m skeptical that if there are some low-propensity voters whose wages are being stretched thin because of Trump’s wars and tariffs that they’re going to care about some cultural issue that doesn't impact their lives,” Stern said. Veteran Republican strategist Charlie Black said the party is right to build on messaging that connected with voters in 2024, and which “might help” in some places, but agreed that "economic issues are predominant this year.” Hack of the Christopher Street Project added there's no one-size-fits-all approach to such a polarizing topic. "We want to make sure that candidates talk about these issues in a way that's inclusive and in a way that makes sense for their individual communities," he said, "and that doesn't always look the exact same."

item.title: Hong Kong's regulators, bourse toughen stance on going-concern disclaimers
item.description: Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing said that it's working with regulators to bolster financial disclosure by requiring listed companies and auditors to resolve going-concern doubts or potentially face trading suspension for financial results without an auditor's opinion.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (0388.HK) said that it's working with regulators to bolster financial disclosure by requiring listed companies and auditors to resolve going-concern doubts or potentially face trading suspension for financial results without an auditor's opinion. The stock exchange operator said on Thursday that the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), the Accounting and Financial Reporting Council (AFRC) and the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong have issued a joint statement that addresses expectations from listed issuers’ management, audit committees and auditors. The joint statement called on listed companies and auditors to strengthen disclosures and oversight of financial statements carrying going-concern disclaimer opinions, amid rising regulatory concerns that such opinions could undermine market quality and investor confidence. A disclaimer of opinion means an auditor has not expressed an opinion on a company's financial statements, raising questions about their reliability. "A disclaimer of opinion, even when it relates solely to going concern, can have significant implications for market quality and investor confidence," HKEX Head of Listing Katherine Ng said. The statement said listed issuers were expected to prepare the going concern assessment and related disclosures carefully, supported by appropriate evidence. The listed companies were also responsible to resolve the underlying going concern issues and should continue to engage proactively with their auditors to address the matters giving rise to the disclaimer of opinion. The three bodies said they would continue to monitor the situation and could take disciplinary, regulatory or enforcement action where misconduct or non-compliance is identified. The exchange would consider modifying the listing rules, including a requirement for listed issuers with disclaimer opinions solely relating to going concern to be suspended, if no significant improvement was observed.

item.title: UK court refuses permission to appeal in diesel emissions lawsuits against carmakers
item.description: London's High Court on Thursday refused claimants permission to appeal against its July decision which broadly found in favour of some of the world's biggest carmakers over diesel emissions.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: London's High Court on Thursday refused claimants permission to appeal against its [USN:L8N43C12G TEXT:"July decision"] which broadly found in favour of some of the world's biggest carmakers over diesel emissions. But lawyers representing around 1.6 million claimants said they would apply directly to the Court of Appeal, in a bid to revive the lawsuits which were brought in the wake of Volkswagen's (VOWG.DE) "Dieselgate" scandal. After a trial, which [USN:L2N3VU08C TEXT:"began in October 2025"], most of the allegations that 20 sample vehicles made by Mercedes-Benz (MBGn.DE) , Ford (F.N) , Nissan (7201.T) , Renault (RENA.PA) and the Stellantis-owned (STLAM.MI) brands Peugeot and Citroen were fitted with unlawful "defeat devices" were rejected. Judge Sara Cockerill refused the claimants permission to appeal against her ruling, though the claimants' lawyers said they would apply directly to the Court of Appeal. She added she would give full reasons for her decision at a later date. Martyn Day, senior partner at one of the claimants' law firms Leigh Day, said: "While we are obviously disappointed with the decision, this is far from the end of the road for the 1.6 million clients bringing a legal claim over Dieselgate."

item.title: Plane damaged at Riyadh airport as Houthis escalate attacks, sources say
item.description: Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis escalated their campaign of strikes against Saudi Arabia on Thursday, trying to shut down the kingdom's airspace and oil facilities with missile fire that has killed three people this week and left a plane badly damaged.
item.dc:creator: Timour Azhari, Federico Maccioni
item.content:encoded: Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis escalated their campaign of strikes against Saudi Arabia on Thursday, trying to shut down the kingdom's airspace and oil facilities with missile fire that has killed three people this week and left a plane badly damaged. The group said it had struck Riyadh airport and warned workers to stay away from energy plants, which would be targeted. Shrapnel from an interception or another projectile hit had left the commercial plane belonging to Saudi state carrier Saudia Airlines heavily damaged after catching fire while parked at an airport terminal on Thursday, three people briefed on the matter said. They said no passengers were believed to have been on the plane at the time but they could not rule out any injuries as a result of the incident. A thick black column of smoke and flames were shown rising from Riyadh airport in video verified by Reuters. Saudi Arabia's government media office, its civil aviation authority and Saudia Airlines did not respond to emailed requests for comment. Lufthansa and Air India said they were [USN:L6N45U10R TEXT:"suspending "]flights to Riyadh after Houthi attacks. Separately, Saudi officials said debris from an intercepted missile had hit a kindergarten and medical complex in Riyadh. The Houthis say they are targeting the kingdom over its support for government forces in Yemen's reignited civil war. Saudi Arabia says it is backing an offensive by Yemen's UN-recognised government to take back territory from the Houthis. The conflict, now an overspill of the US-Iran war , has added new chaos to a region already aflame, and threatens to draw other states into gruelling mountain fighting, with Syria now considering [USN:L1N45U05X TEXT:"deploying troops"] to assist Saudi Arabia. The kingdom has pushed for support from allied nations, including [USN:L6N45T0IX TEXT:"Turkey"] and Pakistan, even if only in a logistical or defensive capacity, as it tries to reverse Houthi gains in southwest Yemen, by the southern entrance to the Red Sea. Those requests have taken on more urgency since Saudi authorities said on Wednesday that three people had been [USN:L1N45T00S TEXT:"killed"] this week in strikes on Riyadh airport and Abha airport in the southwest. DELAYS AND CANCELLATIONS The Houthis have made Saudi airports a focus of their strikes, and the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen said it had destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the group towards Riyadh and another towards Khamis Mushayt, home to a major airbase. According to data compiled by aviation analytics company Cirium, almost half of departures from Riyadh airport had been cancelled by 1500 GMT, with 31 more cancellations expected for Friday in all Saudi airports. Flight tracker FlightRadar24 indicated numerous delayed arrivals and departures at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on Thursday. The airport advised travellers to contact airlines to check the status of flights before trying to travel. Riyadh is due to host a major meeting of energy policy makers, the WPC Energy Congress, this week. Several multinational firms based in Riyadh's King Abdullah Financial District (KAFD) told staff to work from home after loud booms were heard on Thursday morning, five people familiar with the matter said, including some affected staff. The Saudi government did not respond to a request for comment, and KAFD was not immediately available for comment. Some diplomats said they had received warnings, and some schools in Riyadh told parents there were orders to shelter in place, though authorities did not issue a public alert. Reuters could not identify the source of the booms. CIVIL WAR REIGNITED BY CONFLICT IN IRAN Yemen's long-running civil war, which paused with a ceasefire in 2022, has erupted again in recent weeks with the Houthis seizing stretches of the Red Sea coast last month, including along the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Their threats to shipping and attacks on Saudi cities and infrastructure have drawn the kingdom back in. This week, Saudi-backed forces launched a [USN:L8N45M1W0 TEXT:"counterattack"], taking back some areas around the strait. However, in a war with several front lines, the Houthis have made gains of their own, surrounding Yemen's third-largest city, Taiz, by taking territory along its main mountain road to Aden. The fighting, which pits the Houthis against a coalition of [USN:L6N45S0PX TEXT:"Saudi-backed forces"] under the internationally recognised government, has led to a humanitarian crisis in the poorest Arab state, displacing 200,000 people since the conflict resumed. One US and one Syrian defence official said Syria was carefully considering options for military support, including defensive aid to protect Saudi Arabia from attacks, or an offensive deployment to help take the fight to the Houthis. In response to a request for comment to the Syrian foreign ministry, a diplomat said Syria stood firmly with Saudi Arabia but that its focus was on domestic priorities such as recovery from its own civil war. NATO-member Turkey said on Wednesday it was sending mainly defensive and technical support to the kingdom to help in the fight against the Houthis. A Turkish official said this was expected to take the form of military equipment, intelligence sharing and weapons systems.

item.title: Russia says checks following Siberian plague lab death are complete
item.description: Russia said on Thursday it had completed health checks on all the contacts of a deceased lab worker at a plague research facility in Siberia, signalling a desire to draw a line under the affair.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Russia said on Thursday it had completed health checks on all the contacts of a deceased lab worker at a plague research facility in Siberia, signalling a desire to draw a line under the affair. Statements from the [USN:L1N45T08W TEXT:"state health watchdog"] and the regional governor said monitoring of all the dead woman's contacts had concluded, and reiterated that no dangerous pathogens had been found in nearly 5,000 samples. "Amidst intense media scrutiny, the specialists thoroughly investigated the situation. It was a test, but we passed it in worthy fashion," Irkutsk governor Igor Kobzev said. Yet despite pressure from the [USN:L1N45T08W TEXT:"World Health Organization"] (WHO) and the [USN:L8N45S0S6 TEXT:"United States"], Russian authorities have yet to state definitively whether the death of 28-year-old lab worker Darya Shipilova on October 2 could have been caused by [USN:L6N45U0HF TEXT:"plague"]. They have previously stated that she died from pneumonia but that the origin of the pneumonia had yet to be determined. They have also said she was appropriately vaccinated and that no microorganisms linked to her work were found in her body. On Wednesday, senior WHO official Maria Van Kerkhove said the global body wanted more information from Russia on what laboratory tests had been conducted, which pathogens were evaluated and that "if this individual didn't die from plague, then how did she die?" Russia says it has provided full information to the WHO according to established procedures. Global [USN:L4N45T1BB TEXT:"health officials"] - as well as the world's media - have been particularly alert to pneumonia cases of undetermined cause since the COVID-19 pandemic, which began with a cluster of fast-spreading fatal respiratory illness in China. However, the cause of individual pneumonia cases can often not be determined. The lung infection can have a variety of causes other than plague, including other bacterial infections or viral respiratory diseases, such as COVID or flu.

item.title: French students keep up protest pressure with some demonstrations hit by violence
item.description: French teenagers blockaded some high schools and marched through cities on Thursday in the latest wave of nationwide protests about conditions in the country's schools, and some of the demonstrations were marred by violent unrest.
item.dc:creator: Manon Cruz, Dominique Vidalon
item.content:encoded: French teenagers blockaded some high schools and marched through cities on Thursday in the latest wave of nationwide protests about conditions in the country's schools, and some of the demonstrations were marred by violent unrest. The Interior Ministry said 71,500 people participated in the day's demonstrations, of which 24,500 took part in the main Paris protest centred around the Bastille square. The Paris protest was mostly peaceful, although there were occasional clashes between small groups of demonstrators and the police during the evening. Elsewhere, arsonists attacked a [USN:FWN45U1T1 TEXT:"Bordeaux"] police station, a school in Saint-Etienne was ransacked and a teacher in Toulouse was hit by a demonstrator, said the Interior Ministry. In Marseille, police said a teacher at Victor Hugo High School [USN:FWN45U1T4 TEXT:"was attacked"] during the latest protests and has filed a criminal complaint over the incident.
